title: History that Nourishes the Soul
author: Josh Herring
summary: Dr. Josh Herring of the Logres Institute for Classical Liberal Studies presents a lecture delivered at Hillsdale College on what history is and how to teach it in the classical tradition. He opens by rejecting two stereotypes, the Droning Lecturer who loses the whole in minutiae and the Timeline King who equates history with memorising facts. He builds a philosophy of history from Butterfield, Dawson, Lukacs and Oakeshott, arguing that history cultivates compassion for past actors, historical consciousness, and an explanatory story built from surviving remnants. History becomes an application of rhetoric that explores what it means to be human. He offers three pedagogies: primary source annotation, the five C's of change over time, context, contingency, causality and complexity, and Socratic seminars. He concludes that we receive the present as a gift from earlier generations and that teaching history nourishes the souls of teacher and student.
points: Herring rejects the Droning Lecturer and the Timeline King, arguing that neither produces transformation in students.
History is framed as the study of past people with compassion and understanding, asking why actors believed their actions were right rather than simply judging them.
Using Oakeshott's warehouse metaphor, the historian starts from surviving remnants and reconstructs an explanatory story, always provisionally.
History is an application of rhetoric, using available means of persuasion to answer a question about the past as truly as possible.
Three practical pedagogies are primary source annotation, the five C's of historical thinking and a closing Socratic seminar.
quotes: The first stereotype I might call the Droning Lecturer—the antiquarian who focuses on the minutiae of historical detritus, and fails to help students perceive the whole.
When we recognize history for what it is—a limited kind of knowledge that invites the application of rhetoric as we explore what it means to be human—studying and teaching history renews our souls.
The student of history’s goal is not judgment, but understanding.

Rather than “Why did the Crusaders commit moral atrocities?” (which is an excellent question for an ethics course), the student of history asks “Why did the Crusaders believe these moral atrocities were the right course of action?
Rather than a disconnected present, the historically conscious individual sees himself as connected to the persons of both past and future
The historian begins with the remnants, and attempts to reconstruct the whole world within which the fragments existed. Such a construction is always limited, and subject to change.
History thus becomes an application of rhetoric - the use of all available means of persuasion, to answer a question as truly as possible.
The study of history operates rather like the description of a will - by studying history, you learn what you have inherited. What you make of that inheritance is up to you.
Causality rarely has one and only one answer, and for that reason it is closely connected to complexity.
